newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-TITLE RACE HOTS UP AT HOCKENHEIM.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-TITLE RACE HOTS UP AT HOCKENHEIM.

text.p: Formula One leader Michael Schumacher will hope that Ferrari have cured the reliability problems which dogged them at Silverstone two weeks ago as he bids for a home victory in the German Grand Prix at Hockenheim on Sunday.

The double world champion, who was forced out of the lead in the British Grand Prix with a wheel-bearing failure, enters the German race with a four-point lead over Canadian Jacques Villeneuve as the championship enters its second half.

"The car went a lot better than I thought it would at Silverstone," Schumacher said. "It was just unfortunate that a wheel-bearing failure took away my chance of pulling even further ahead in the championship.

"It was my first mechanical non-finish this season, so I really cannot complain. Last year was a lot worse. It's thanks to the great reliability we have had this year and the progress the team has made that we have still got a four-point lead."
Schumacher became the first German to win the German Grand Prix in 1995 but last year finished fifth behind the Williams of Briton Damon Hill.
This year Villeneuve carries the British team's hopes of success and aims to maintain momentum following his victory at Silverstone, the 100th win for Williams.
"The battle with Ferrari will be interesting," Villeneuve said. "Ferrari has a strong engine now. They will be strong in Germany but so will we.
"Hockenheim is a similar track to Montreal and we were competitive there so I don't see any reason why we won't be quick in Germany."

Villeneuve's German team mate Heinz-Harald Frentzen, who has had a disappointing first half, will be keen to perform well at home amid rumours that he is under pressure to keep his seat for next year.
After his opening-lap retirement at Silverstone, Frentzen said: "I now know how it feels to make a mistake at Williams.
"I knew this time would come, so I'm glad it is out of the way so I can get on with putting the record straight and scoring some good world championship points."

The German Grand Prix will mark the return of Gerhard Berger after a three-race absence due to sinus problems. Berger's temporary replacement, fellow Austrian Alexander Wurz, will be forced to the sidelines despite finishing third in the British Grand Prix.
Benetton's technical director Pat Symonds was confident that Berger and French team mate Jean Alesi would rediscover the form which enabled them to challenge for victory last season.
"Alexander did a great job while he was here but Gerhard is a fantastic driver with a lot of experience and we are pleased to welcome him back," Symonds said.
"After coming within three laps of victory last season, I hope he can finish the job this Sunday."
The home fans will also be keeping a close eye on the third German driver, Ralf Schumacher, Michael's younger brother. The Jordan racer will be competing in his first home grand prix.
"I am really looking forward to racing in Germany," he said. "I am hoping the fans will be able to motivate me even further to have a good race. I very much hope to win points again this weekend.
Reigning world champion Damon Hill can expect at most a points finish. The British driver took sixth place at Silverstone and anticipates a similar result in the intense atmosphere of Hockenheim.

"Out there you are on your own for much of the lap and then you come back into this enormous stadium section where all the people are," he said. "On the first lap of the race when they come into view, you can feel the excitement."

The Hockenheim circuit, 80 kilometres south of Frankfurt, includes a flat-out section through forest, where cars reach speeds of more than 320 kph, followed by a twisty stadium section where more than 120,000 fans cram into the grandstands.
The race, which starts at 1300 GMT, is run over 45 laps of the 6.823-km circuit.
